title: Budgeting & Resource Management
description: Estimate and control project costs with EVM, reserves, and cost types, and allocate people sensibly.

questions.prompt: At the month-3 status review: planned value (PV) = $60,000, earned value (EV) = $50,000, actual cost (AC) = $45,000. What is the project's status?

options.text: Behind schedule and under budget
Ahead of schedule and over budget
Behind schedule and over budget
Ahead of schedule and under budget

questions.explanation: SV = EV - PV = -$10,000 (SPI 0.83, behind schedule) and CV = EV - AC = +$5,000 (CPI 1.11, under budget). A common mistake is comparing AC with PV, which mixes spending with the plan and says nothing about the value of the work done.

questions.prompt: A company stops buying on-premises servers, which it depreciated over five years, and moves the workloads to pay-as-you-go cloud instances billed monthly. How does this typically change the accounting treatment of that infrastructure spend?

options.text: It shifts spend from operating expense to capital expense
No change, because IT infrastructure is always a capital expense
It shifts spend from capital expense to operating expense
The monthly bills are capitalised and depreciated over five years

questions.explanation: Purchased servers are capital assets depreciated over their useful life (capex); pay-as-you-go usage fees are expensed in the period incurred (opex). That shift is one reason finance teams treat cloud migrations as a budgeting change, not just a technical one.

questions.prompt: The risk register lists "Vendor raises license prices at renewal," and $40,000 was set aside for it. The vendor then announces an increase that will cost the project $30,000. Where should the money come from?

options.text: Management reserve, after the sponsor approves the release
Contingency reserve, which is already part of the cost baseline
A change request to raise the budget at completion (BAC)
Cutting scope elsewhere so the cost baseline is not touched

questions.explanation: Contingency reserve covers identified risks (known-unknowns) and is included in the cost baseline, so the PM can apply it under the project's procedures. Management reserve is for unidentified risks (unknown-unknowns) and sits outside the cost baseline.

questions.prompt: True or false: When deciding whether to continue a troubled project, the $2 million already spent on it is a valid reason to keep funding it.
questions.explanation: Money already spent is a sunk cost: it cannot be recovered whichever way you decide. Continue-or-stop decisions should compare the remaining cost (ETC) with the remaining expected benefits. Letting past spend drive the decision is the sunk-cost fallacy.

questions.prompt: To budget a laptop refresh, an analyst uses last quarter's average fully configured cost of $1,350 per workstation and multiplies by the 85 workstations in scope: $114,750. Which estimating technique is this?

options.text: Analogous estimating
Bottom-up estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating

questions.explanation: Parametric estimating multiplies a statistical unit rate by a quantity ($/unit x units). Analogous estimating would scale the whole cost of a similar past project without a unit rate, and bottom-up estimating would sum separate estimates for each item.

questions.prompt: A project has BAC = $500,000, EV = $200,000, and AC = $250,000. The cost overruns come from systemic underestimation that is expected to continue. What is the estimate to complete (ETC)?
questions.explanation: CPI = 200,000 / 250,000 = 0.8; with typical variances EAC = BAC / CPI = $625,000, so ETC = EAC - AC = $375,000. $300,000 (BAC - EV) assumes future work goes to plan, which contradicts the stated assumption, and $625,000 is the EAC, not the ETC.

questions.prompt: A project shows BAC = $800,000, PV = $400,000, EV = $350,000, AC = $420,000. The overrun came from a one-time vendor penalty that will not recur, and the remaining work is expected to be done at the budgeted rate. What is the variance at completion (VAC)?
questions.explanation: For atypical variance, EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) = 420,000 + 450,000 = $870,000, so VAC = BAC - EAC = -$70,000. Using BAC / CPI (CPI = 0.833, EAC = $960,000) gives -$160,000, which wrongly assumes the overrun will continue; -$50,000 is the schedule variance.

questions.prompt: Here is next week's resource allocation (hours). Lena works a 0.8 FTE schedule. Which statement is correct?

code.source:
Person  Project A  Project B  Ops/BAU  Weekly capacity
Priya   24         20         8        40
Marco   16         16         4        40
Lena    30         0          10       32
Tom     20         12         8        40

options.text: Only Priya is over-allocated, by 12 hours
Priya, Lena, and Tom are all over-allocated
Lena is the most over-allocated, by 10 hours
Priya (by 12 hours) and Lena (by 8 hours) are over-allocated

questions.explanation: Priya has 52 h against 40 (+12) and Lena has 40 h against her 32 h capacity (+8); Tom is at exactly 100% and Marco is at 36 h. Missing Lena's reduced capacity is the usual mistake, and Tom being fully loaded does not make him over-allocated.

questions.prompt: A consulting firm is building the budget for a client CRM implementation. Which of these are direct costs of the project? Select all that apply.

options.text: Contractor hours billed to the CRM implementation
Software licenses bought solely for this client's CRM
A share of the firm's headquarters office rent
Salaries of the firm's corporate HR department
Travel to the client site for this project's user acceptance testing

questions.explanation: Direct costs can be traced specifically to the project: its contractor hours, licenses, and project travel. Office rent and corporate HR salaries are shared overhead (indirect costs) that may be allocated to the project through an overhead rate, but they are not caused by it.

questions.prompt: A team of 6 FTEs has a fully loaded cost of $12,000 per FTE per month, plus $8,000 per month in tooling. $400,000 of budget remains and the forecast shows 6 months of work left. How many months can be funded, and what is the shortfall?

options.text: 5 months; shortfall of $80,000
6 months; no shortfall
4 months; shortfall of $160,000
5.5 months; shortfall of $40,000

questions.explanation: Monthly burn = 6 x $12,000 + $8,000 = $80,000; $400,000 / $80,000 = 5 months, and 6 months of work needs $480,000, a $80,000 shortfall. Leaving out tooling gives a $72,000 burn and about 5.6 months, which hides most of the gap.

questions.prompt: A project has BAC = $1,000,000, EV = $400,000, and AC = $500,000. The sponsor insists the original budget will still be met. Which calculation and conclusion are correct?

options.text: TCPI = 0.80; the remaining work can be done at the current efficiency
TCPI = 1.25; the team must be 25% more efficient than it has been so far
TCPI = 1.20, far above the current CPI of 0.80, so meeting BAC is unrealistic
TCPI = 0.83; there is slack in the remaining budget to absorb the overrun

questions.explanation: TCPI (to BAC) = (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) = 600,000 / 500,000 = 1.20; the team would need $1.20 of work per $1 spent for the rest of the project, while it has achieved $0.80. 0.80 is the CPI, not the TCPI, and 0.83 is the TCPI ratio inverted.

questions.prompt: Status: BAC = $1,200,000, PV = $600,000, EV = $480,000, AC = $600,000. Leadership has made the original end date mandatory, so schedule pressure (overtime, expediting) is expected to drive the remaining cost along with current cost performance. Which EAC fits this assumption?
questions.explanation: CPI = SPI = 0.8. When both cost and schedule performance affect the remaining work, EAC = AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI x SPI) = 600,000 + 720,000 / 0.64 = $1,725,000. $1,500,000 (BAC / CPI) ignores the schedule factor, and $1,875,000 wrongly applies CPI x SPI to the whole BAC, including work already done.

questions.prompt: On a large program, EV is calculated from the percent complete that task owners report. Several 6-week work packages have been reported as "90% complete" for four weeks, and the CPI looks healthy at 1.02. What change makes the EVM data reliable?

options.text: None, since subjective estimates tend to average out over many packages
Report only actual cost, since spending data is objective and trustworthy
Collect owners' percent-complete estimates weekly instead of monthly
Measure EV with 0/100 or 50/50 rules or objective milestones

questions.explanation: Self-reported percent complete runs optimistic (the "90% syndrome"), which inflates EV and makes CPI and SPI look better than reality. Fixed-formula rules (0/100, 50/50) for short packages, or weighted milestones with objective completion criteria, tie EV to verifiable progress; asking more often does not remove the bias.

questions.prompt: The company's only senior DBA is allocated 33% to each of three projects, and all three are now late waiting on database work. Each project's remaining database work is a fixed number of hours. Which allocation change will most likely get the most value delivered soonest?

options.text: Sequence the DBA's work by portfolio priority, finishing one project before the next
Keep the 33% split but require detailed daily timesheets for each project
Give each project 40% of the DBA's time so they all move faster
Rotate the DBA between projects every day so each gets equal attention

questions.explanation: Even before counting context-switching overhead, a three-way split makes all three projects finish near the same late date, while working in priority order finishes the top project after about a third of that time and the last one no later than before; switching overhead only widens the gap. A 40% x 3 allocation is 120% over-allocation, and daily rotation adds more switching.

questions.prompt: Halfway through, a new regulation that no one foresaw requires $120,000 of extra in-scope work. Contingency is reserved for specific risks on the register. How should this be funded?

options.text: From contingency reserve, which the PM can authorize without anyone else
From management reserve once approved, adding it to the cost baseline
From management reserve drawn by the PM, leaving the cost baseline unchanged
Absorbed as a negative cost variance against the current cost baseline

questions.explanation: An unforeseen event (unknown-unknown) is what management reserve is for; it sits outside the cost baseline, requires management approval, and once used is added to the cost baseline through an approved change (PMBOK). Leaving the baseline unchanged would make EVM report a false cost overrun.
